sanctuary.justification:
Reasoning:
1. The claim, made by Paresh Rawal on October 29, 2020, asserts that Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) was removed from the United Nations' list of "unresolved disputes."
2. The evidence presents a direct contradiction regarding the validity of this claim. Evidence Q1, A1 (Economic Times) reports that J&K was indeed omitted from a list of unresolved disputes, which was viewed as a setback by Pakistan. However, Evidence Q1, A2 and Q1, A3 (Dawn) clarify that the UN Security Council still maintains the mandate of the United Nations Military Observer Group in India and Pakistan (UNMOGIP) in the region and continues to treat the area as an unresolved dispute on the Security Council's agenda. Furthermore, Evidence Q1, A6 (Dawn) features a UN diplomat stating that an agenda item can only be closed by a consensus decision of the Security Council, which has not occurred.
3. There is a clear conflict between the "omission" noted in a specific list (which may have been an inadvertent administrative error, as suggested in Q1, A5) and the official legal/procedural status of the dispute within the UN Security Council. The claim relies on a specific instance of omission from a list, while the broader UN framework and military presence (UNMOGIP) confirm the dispute remains active and unresolved.
4. Because the evidence shows that while an omission was observed in a specific context (supporting the literal observation of the claim), the UN's official stance and procedural actions (UNMOGIP and Security Council agenda) directly contradict the implication that the dispute is "resolved" or "removed" from the UN's oversight, the evidence is conflicting. The claim is a result of cherrypicking a specific administrative omission while ignoring the broader, ongoing UN mandate.

infact.justification: The United Nations did not remove Jammu and Kashmir from its agenda of unresolved disputes; rather, the [UN Security Council continues to treat the region as an unresolved dispute](https://www.dawn.com/news/1578012) and maintains military observers on both sides of the Line of Control. While there were reports of an "omission" from certain lists, diplomats characterized this as an inadvertent error rather than a formal change in status, and the [UN position remains governed by Security Council resolutions](https://news.un.org/en/story/2019/08/1044401) which recognize the territory as a contested area.
